An example is an organised initiative taking place in ${survey_year} that includes, or solely focuses on, improving or producing national statistics on refugees, IDPs and/or stateless people. It can be a data source such as a census, a survey, an administrative database or an integration of several sources, or a tool such as a workshop, a training, a strategic document, guidance or a toolkit. A current example is one that is ongoing at the time of this survey, meaning some time, capacity, staffing or financial investment has been made. It does not have to be finished.

What the recommendations were used for. This question is asked once per recommendation you selected, because each one may have been used differently. Including in a population census means the groups were counted or identified within a census. Including in a sample survey means either added to a survey of the national population, or covered by a stand-alone survey. Government administrative data means registers or records held by a public authority. Operational data from humanitarian organisations means data generated through humanitarian operations. Non-traditional data sources means satellite imagery, mobile phone data, social media and similar. Coordinating and planning means working arrangements, mandates, strategies or planning across institutions.

Which parts of the recommendations were actually used. Statistical framework or population group means the definitions and population categories. Recommendations on data sources means guidance on which sources to use and how. Coordination means arrangements between institutions. Data sharing means protocols or agreements for exchanging data. Analysis means analytical approaches and comparisons. Indicator selection means choosing which indicators to produce. Data integration means combining sources. Dissemination means how results are published and communicated. Institutional or sectoral strategy means embedding them in a strategy or plan.
A few sentences is enough. Type NA if there is nothing to add.

Identification questions are the questions asked in a survey or census to establish whether a person is a refugee, an internally displaced person, or stateless. They are the questions in the instrument itself, not the classification applied afterwards in processing.
Please select all that apply.

Forced to flee asks whether the person left their usual home because of conflict, violence, persecution, human rights violations or disaster. Habitual residency asks where the person usually lived before, and is used to establish displacement within the country. Crossing a border asks whether the person crossed an international border. Citizenship asks the country of citizenship, or whether the person holds any. International protection asks whether the person holds refugee status or another form of international protection.

████████████████████████████████████████████ Challenges with the example itself The next questions ask about difficulties in carrying out this example, whatever their cause.

Challenges are significant difficulties encountered during an example: coverage gaps, collection errors, difficulty identifying the populations, confidentiality concerns, resource constraints and technical skill gaps. This question is about the example as a whole. PRO21, further down, asks separately about difficulties in applying the EGRISS recommendations.

████████████████████████████████████████████ Challenges in using the recommendations These questions are not about the example. They ask whether the EGRISS recommendations themselves were difficult to apply.
This is what tells EGRISS where the recommendations are hard to use in practice, and it feeds the guidance and training produced next year. Please be as candid as you can.

A future example is one for which no significant investment has yet been made in design, budgeting, training, listing or enumeration. Plans count even if funding is not confirmed. This section is used to anticipate where support may be needed, not to hold you to a commitment.
